title: Destroy vs Parent = nil
summary: Setting Parent = nil hides an instance but keeps it alive and reusable. Destroy() kills it and all descendants PERMANENTLY — Parent is locked, re-parenting errors. Choose deliberately.

explanation.whatItIs: Two ways to remove: park it (nil) or burn it (Destroy). Only one is reversible.
explanation.whyItExists: Object pooling wants reversibility; garbage wants finality. Both are legitimate.
symptoms: 'The Parent property of X is locked' when re-parenting
Objects disappearing from memory tools faster than expected (destroy cascades)
'Hidden' objects still firing events (they're parked, not dead)
explanation.fix: Destroy for true removal (+ disconnect YOUR connections to it). Parent=nil for pooling/soft-hiding. Never Destroy what you'll reuse.
tips: Destroyed objects still respond to SOME calls — don't rely on them erroring loudly
Pool expensive templates with Clone-on-demand instead of destroy/recreate
commonMistakes: Destroying then later setting Parent expecting revival
Parent=nil and wondering why memory didn't drop (it's still referenced)
Forgetting connections to destroyed objects keep firing on events that still exist elsewhere

examples.title: Pool vs burn
examples.code:
-- Soft-hide for reuse:
local bullet = spawnBullet()
bullet.Parent = nil            -- parked
-- later:
bullet.Parent = workspace      -- back! (still configured)

-- Permanent:
local trash = Instance.new("Part")
trash.Parent = workspace
trash:Destroy()
-- trash.Parent = workspace     ← ERROR: locked

-- Pooling pattern:
local pool = {}
local function release(obj)
    obj.Parent = nil
    table.insert(pool, obj)
end
local function acquire()
    return table.remove(pool) or createNew()
end
